newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila stock market hounded by property fears.
newsitem.headline: Manila stock market hounded by property fears.

text.p: Concerns over a glut in the Philippine property sector won't go away quickly and are likely to continue to cast a pall on the local stock market, analysts said on Friday.
"To most foreign fund managers, this property glut is an issue and investors would rather play it safe and stay out of the sector," said Pamela Pena, analyst at Citisecurities Inc.

"People will be cautious and defensive on property issues for the rest of the year. The negative sentiment surrounding the property sector may still yank blue chip Ayala Land to even cheaper levels," Noel Reyes, research head at Anscor Hagedorn Securities Inc.

BPI Securities Corp analyst Bernadette Tamayo said concerns of a glut on the local property sector started last year. It was aggravated by the slump in Thailand's real estate business that adversely affected banking stocks.

"We see a lot of comparisons with Thailand and the exposure of banks that have the biggest market capitalisation here had affected the stock market negatively," said Cilette Liboro, vice-president for research at Orion-Squire Capital Inc.
Local bank loan portfolios are estimated to have about 10 to 11 percent exposure to property companies.
The recent debt problems of Victorias Milling Co, though the result of different factors, have only underlined the issue of problem loans, analysts said.
Rising interest rates in the U.S. have also led to a sell-off in the sector.

Recent rumours that companies Megaworld Properties & Holdings Inc and unit Empire East Land Holdings Inc were cash-strapped also dampened sentiment towards the sector despite repeated denials by the companies.

"Even Ayala Land which is the McDonalds of the property sector has acknowledged that it needs to rework some of its projects, experiencing trouble selling them so what more the other smaller companies," Reyes said.

Ayala Land Inc president Francisco Licuanan earlier said that an oversupply in luxury apartments may come about in 1999. Ayala said it will put emphasis on the burgeoning middle-income housing market.

Joey Salceda, director at SBC Warburg said: "Aggressive underweighting of the properties and the banks remain the central theme to foreign investors. Although we may see some buybacks and nibbling on the side, people are still vomiting."
